name: NIH Office of Data Science Strategy: AI Programs in Biomedical Research
title: NIH Office of Data Science Strategy: AI Programs in Biomedical Research
answer: The NIH Office of Data Science Strategy funds AI and machine learning research across biomedical science through administrative supplement programs, covering data readiness, ethics and workforce development. Its most useful contribution is a detailed record of funded projects, including a convolutional neural network that detects neuronal death from cell images alone, showing how NIH money turns into clinical AI methods.

sections.body: This is the artificial intelligence section of datascience.nih.gov, published by the National Institutes of Health Office of Data Science Strategy. It consists of programme pages describing administrative supplement funding notices and listing the awardee projects they produced. The pages cover notices issued between 2021 and 2023, including NOT-OD-21-079, NOT-OD-21-094, NOT-OD-22-065, NOT-OD-22-067 and NOT-OD-23-082, along with records of principal investigator meetings held in 2021, 2022 and 2024. The material is a public account of how NIH organises and reports its AI research funding rather than a scientific paper or clinical guidance.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The Office of Data Science Strategy has run successive rounds of administrative supplements to build AI and machine learning capacity in biomedical and behavioural research. The first cohort in 2021 split into two themes, workforce development at the interface of information sciences, AI and machine learning and biomedical sciences, and collaborations to improve the AI/ML-readiness of NIH-supported data. Twenty-four workforce awards went to investigators at 23 institutes in summer 2021. A 2022 ethics notice, NOT-OD-22-065, produced 22 awards at 33 institutions, and a 2023 readiness notice, NOT-OD-23-082, produced 34 awards at 15 institutions, following 36 awards under the 2022 readiness notice. The pages describe individual projects in some detail. One develops a genetically encoded cell death indicator and a convolutional neural network trained on automatically generated image data, which detects neuronal death from morphology alone without further use of the biosensor. Others address bias in imaging analysis, cognitive impairment screening, prostate and head and neck cancer imaging databases, and community perspectives on AI in mobile health. The recurring aim is to make NIH-funded data findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable, and ready for machine learning.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source states that 24 workforce awards were made in summer 2021 to investigators at 23 institutes, 22 ethics awards in 2022 to investigators at 33 institutions, 36 readiness awards in 2022 to investigators at 33 institutions, and 34 readiness awards in 2023 to investigators at 15 institutions. It gives notice numbers NOT-OD-21-079, NOT-OD-21-094, NOT-OD-22-065, NOT-OD-22-067 and NOT-OD-23-082, and dates including the February 3, 2022 announcement of the ethics notice and its April 1, 2022 expiry. It names Susan Gregurick as Associate Director for Data Science and ODSS Director, appointed September 16, 2019, and Laura Biven as lead of the Integrated Infrastructure and Emerging Technologies branch.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For anyone following AI in healthcare, this source shows the funding machinery behind much clinical AI research. It documents which problems NIH chose to pay for, from data readiness and ethics to workforce training, and names the institutions and investigators doing the work. The project descriptions give concrete examples of clinical AI in development, including deep learning for neuronal death detection, automated cognitive impairment screening and multi-scale MRI databases for prostate cancer. It is a record of research infrastructure and intent rather than of deployed clinical tools, but it is the layer that produces the datasets and methods later clinical AI depends on.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Healthcare

sections.body: The pages are programme administration rather than evaluation. They list awards, titles and meeting agendas but give no results, performance data or clinical outcomes from the funded projects. Coverage stops at the 2024 principal investigator meeting, and several project descriptions are truncated mid-sentence. The material is confined to NIH ODSS supplement programmes, so it does not survey AI in healthcare more broadly, and it offers no regulatory guidance or product information.
